---
id: cpp-prefix-evaluator
title: Prefix Expression Evaluator
difficulty: Medium
order: 7
tags: recursion, parsing, expressions, error handling
time_limit: 1
---
## Statement
In **prefix (Polish) notation** the operator comes before its operands: `+ 2 3` means 2 + 3, and `* + 1 2 - 9 4` means (1 + 2) × (9 − 4) = 15. No parentheses are needed.

The grammar is recursive: an expression is either a number, or an operator followed by **two expressions**.

```cpp
std::string evaluate(const std::string& expr);
```

- Tokens are separated by single spaces. Numbers are non-negative integers below 10⁹. Operators are `+ - * /`, where `/` is integer division truncating toward zero, as in C++.
- Return the value as a string. All intermediate values fit in `long long`.
- Return `"invalid"` if the expression is malformed: an operator runs out of operands, or tokens are left over after a complete expression.
- Return `"division by zero"` if a division by zero is evaluated, **unless** the expression is malformed (check the structure first).

**Input:** one expression per line, up to 10⁵ tokens. Nesting can reach 5·10⁴ levels deep.

## Starter
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

string evaluate(const string& expr) {
    return "invalid";
}
```

## Driver
```cpp
int main() {
    string line;
    while (getline(cin, line)) cout << evaluate(line) << '\n';
}
```

## Hints
- Split the line into tokens first. Then `expr()` takes the next token: a number returns itself, and an operator calls `expr()` twice.
- Read the left and right operands into two separate variables, one statement each.
- If you run out of tokens, mark the expression invalid. After the top-level `expr()`, every token must have been used.

## Solution
The grammar gives the code directly: `expr()` reads one token. A number is the base case. An operator recursively reads its left expression, then its right expression, then combines them.

The two operands are read in **separate statements** (`long long a = expr(); long long b = expr();`), so the left one is guaranteed to consume its tokens first. Writing `apply(t, expr(), expr())` would be a bug, because C++ doesn't specify argument evaluation order.

**Errors:**

- Running out of tokens sets `malformed`.
- After the top-level call, any unread tokens also mean malformed.
- Division by zero sets a flag but keeps parsing, so a malformed expression is still reported as `invalid` first.

The nesting depth here is at most 5·10⁴ frames, which is safe. For depths of 10⁶ you'd evaluate right-to-left with an explicit stack instead (push numbers, and an operator pops two).

Complexity: O(number of tokens).

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Eval {
    vector<string> tok; size_t i = 0;
    bool malformed = false, divzero = false;

    long long expr() {
        if (i >= tok.size()) { malformed = true; return 0; }
        const string& t = tok[i++];
        if (isdigit((unsigned char)t[0])) return stoll(t);        // base case: a number
        long long a = expr();                 // left operand (evaluated first, in order)
        long long b = expr();                 // right operand
        if (malformed) return 0;
        switch (t[0]) {
            case '+': return a + b;
            case '-': return a - b;
            case '*': return a * b;
            default:
                if (b == 0) { divzero = true; return 0; }
                return a / b;
        }
    }
};

string evaluate(const string& expr) {
    Eval e;
    istringstream in(expr);
    for (string t; in >> t; ) e.tok.push_back(t);
    long long v = e.expr();
    if (e.malformed || e.i != e.tok.size()) return "invalid";
    if (e.divzero) return "division by zero";
    return to_string(v);
}
```
